key_terms.meaning: The baseband information waveform m(t) produced by the source, for example speech, audio or a sensor voltage.
A signal whose spectrum starts at or near 0 Hz and extends to some maximum frequency W.
A high-frequency sinusoid A·cos(2πf_c t + φ) used only to carry the message through the channel; it holds no information of its own.
The physical medium between transmitter and receiver: wire, coaxial cable, optical fibre, free space, or an underwater acoustic path.
A radiating antenna is practical at about λ/4; for a 1 kHz tone λ = 300 km, so the antenna would be about 75 km tall.
Sharing one channel by placing several messages in different frequency slots (FDM) or time slots (TDM); this needs a carrier to define the slots.
X(f) = ∫ x(t)·e^(−j2πft) dt; it gives the complex amplitude density at each frequency f, in volts per hertz.
A signal whose spectrum is confined to |f| between f_c − B/2 and f_c + B/2, with B much smaller than f_c.
x̂(t) = x(t) ∗ 1/(πt); it shifts every frequency component by −90 degrees and keeps the magnitude unchanged.
x₊(t) = x(t) + j·x̂(t); it contains only the positive-frequency half of the spectrum of x(t).
x̃(t) = x₊(t)·e^(−j2πf_c t) = x_I(t) + j·x_Q(t), the baseband equivalent of a band-pass signal.
A rule X that assigns a real number to each outcome of an experiment; its measured value is described by a CDF or PDF.
F_X(x) = P(X ≤ x) is the cumulative probability; f_X(x) = dF_X/dx is the density, so P(a < X ≤ b) = ∫ f_X(x) dx from a to b.
X(t, ζ): an ensemble of signal waveforms indexed by time, where ζ labels one sample waveform of the experiment.
A process whose mean is constant and whose autocorrelation R_X(τ) depends only on the time difference τ, not on t.
R_X(τ) = E[X(t)·X(t+τ)], the average product of the process with a shifted copy of itself; R_X(0) equals the mean power.
S_X(f) = ∫ R_X(τ)·e^(−j2πfτ) dτ, in watts per hertz; power in a band is the integral of S_X(f) over that band.
A process whose PSD is flat, S(f) = N₀/2 W/Hz for all f, giving autocorrelation (N₀/2)·δ(τ).
Additive white Gaussian noise: the noise voltage adds to the signal, has a flat spectrum, and its amplitude has a Gaussian PDF.
F = SNR_in/SNR_out as a linear ratio; in decibels NF = 10·log₁₀ F.
T_e = (F − 1)·T₀ with T₀ = 290 K, the temperature of a matched resistor that would add the same noise.

takeaways: A communication system is source, transmitter, channel, receiver and destination; the channel always adds noise and limits bandwidth, so the design goal is to keep error small at low power and low cost.

Modulation exists for four practical reasons: antenna size at f_c, frequency assignment by a regulator, multiplexing many users on one medium, and moving the signal to a band where noise and interference are easier to handle.
The Fourier transform turns filtering, modulation and bandwidth into multiplication and shifting in the frequency domain, which is why it is the main tool of the subject.
A narrowband band-pass signal needs only its complex envelope x̃(t), a low-pass pair (x_I, x_Q), because the carrier f_c is known and can be put back at the receiver.
The Hilbert transform supplies the 90-degree shifted version of a signal, so every real band-pass signal has the canonical form x_c(t)cos(2πf_c t) − x_s(t)sin(2πf_c t).
CDF and PDF answer the only question a receiver really asks: what is the probability that the measured value falls past a decision threshold?
For a WSS random process the autocorrelation R_X(τ) describes power in time and its Fourier transform S_X(f) describes power in frequency; the pair is the Wiener–Khinchine relation.
White noise is a model, not a physical signal: it has infinite power, so it is always used with a finite bandwidth, and over that band the power is N₀B.
Cascaded stages are dominated by the first stage: Friis gives F_total = F₁ + (F₂ − 1)/G₁ + (F₃ − 1)/(G₁G₂) + …, which is why the front-end amplifier sets receiver sensitivity.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually ask for a labelled block diagram plus a derivation — the band-pass to low-pass conversion, the Wiener–Khinchine relation, or a noise-figure/SNR calculation — so show the steps and keep the units on every power and temperature term.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a communication system and explain, with numbers, why modulation is needed.
outline: Source, transducer, modulator, transmitter, channel with added noise, receiver, demodulator, output transducer, destination.
Antenna size argument: λ = c/f, quarter-wave rule, 1 kHz needs about 75 km, 100 MHz needs about 0.75 m.
Frequency assignment: regulators allot bands, unmodulated baseband cannot be allocated.
Multiplexing: many messages share one channel by frequency or time slots.
Noise and interference: shifting to a chosen band allows filtering and better SNR.
Bandwidth: modulation trades bandwidth for noise immunity; mention baseband versus passband.

bank.q: State the Fourier transform and its inverse, and explain the four properties that are used most in modulation analysis.
outline: Definition X(f) = ∫x(t)e^(−j2πft)dt and inverse x(t) = ∫X(f)e^(j2πft)df.
Linearity.
Frequency-shift (modulation) theorem: x(t)cos(2πf_c t) gives half the spectrum moved to ±f_c.
Convolution theorem: time convolution equals frequency multiplication, the basis of filtering.
Parseval/Rayleigh energy relation and the units of X(f).

bank.q: Define a random variable, its CDF and its PDF, and give the expressions for mean and variance.
outline: Random variable as a mapping from outcomes to real numbers.
Properties of F_X: non-decreasing, limits 0 and 1, right-continuous.
f_X = dF_X/dx, total area one, P(a < X ≤ b) as an integral.
Mean m = ∫x f_X(x)dx and variance σ² = ∫(x − m)² f_X(x)dx = E[X²] − m².
Gaussian PDF as the standard example with its mean and variance parameters.

bank.q: Define a wide-sense stationary process and state the Wiener–Khinchine theorem with the properties of the autocorrelation function.
outline: Ensemble, time average versus ensemble average, definition of WSS (constant mean, R depends only on τ).
Properties: R(0) = mean power, R(−τ) = R(τ), |R(τ)| ≤ R(0), R(∞) equals mean squared.
Wiener–Khinchine: S_X(f) = F{R_X(τ)}, with the inverse relation.
S_X(f) is real, even and non-negative; power in a band is its integral.
Note that WSS does not imply Gaussian and does not imply ergodic.

bank.q: Define noise figure and noise temperature, relate them, and write the Friis formula for cascaded stages.
outline: F = SNR_in/SNR_out for a matched source at T₀ = 290 K; NF = 10 log₁₀ F.
T_e = (F − 1)T₀ and F = 1 + T_e/T₀.
Friis: F = F₁ + (F₂ − 1)/G₁ + (F₃ − 1)/(G₁G₂) + … and the temperature form.
Meaning: the first stage and its gain control the overall figure.
Lossy component has F equal to its loss when at T₀.

bank.q: A band-pass signal is x(t) = A·m(t)·cos(2πf_c t) with m(t) band-limited to W hertz and W much less than f_c. Find its Hilbert transform, analytic signal, complex envelope, and sketch the spectra.
outline: Hilbert transform of cos is sin, so x̂(t) = A·m(t)·sin(2πf_c t).
Analytic signal x₊ = A·m(t)·[cos + j sin] = A·m(t)·e^(j2πf_c t).
Complex envelope x̃(t) = A·m(t), purely real, so x_Q = 0.
Spectrum: two sidebands at ±f_c of width 2W each; analytic signal keeps the positive part only.
State the condition W ≪ f_c for the narrowband approximation and the resulting bandwidth 2W.

bank.q: White noise of two-sided PSD N₀/2 = 10⁻²⁰ W/Hz passes through an ideal band-pass filter of bandwidth B = 1 MHz centred at 100 MHz. Find the output noise power and the SNR if the signal power at the filter output is 1 pW.
outline: Output noise power = N₀B with N₀ the one-sided density.
SNR = 10⁻¹²/2 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 50, that is about 17 dB.
Remark that only the noise inside the filter band matters.
Keep units: W/Hz × Hz = W.

bank.q: A receiver is an RF amplifier (G₁ = 20 dB, F₁ = 2) followed by a mixer (G₂ = 10 dB, F₂ = 10) and an IF amplifier (F₃ = 4). Compute the overall noise figure in decibels.
outline: Convert gains from dB to ratios: G₁ = 100, G₂ = 10.
NF = 10 log₁₀ 2.093 ≈ 3.2 dB.
Comment that the later stages contribute almost nothing because of the preceding gain.

bank.q: A stationary process has autocorrelation R_X(τ) = P·e^(−a|τ|) with a > 0. Find its power spectral density and the power in the band |f| ≤ a/2π.
outline: Apply Wiener–Khinchine as a two-sided exponential transform.
S_X(f) = 2aP/(a² + 4π²f²).
Check total power: ∫S_X(f)df = P = R_X(0).
Band power by integrating S_X(f) over the stated limits, giving a power in watts.
Note S_X(0) = 2P/a and that the spectrum is not flat, unlike white noise.

bank.q: Explain why an ideal white noise source cannot exist in practice, and show how the concept is still used with a finite bandwidth and equivalent noise bandwidth.
outline: Flat PSD for all f means infinite total power, so it is a mathematical model for noise whose spectrum is flat over the band of interest.
Real sources are flat only up to a physical limit, often kTB with k the Boltzmann constant.
Band-limiting: power = N₀B over the filter bandwidth B.
Equivalent noise bandwidth definition through the filter magnitude squared integral, and its use for non-rectangular filters.
Consequence: only noise within the receiver band matters; wider bandwidth means more noise, which explains the bandwidth-for-SNR trade-off.

bank.q: Explain the complex-envelope or low-pass equivalent approach for band-pass signals and systems, and show why it simplifies the analysis of modulation, filtering and noise.
outline: Start from the analytic signal and shift by f_c to obtain x̃(t).
Canonical form x(t) = x_I(t)cos(2πf_c t) − x_Q(t)sin(2πf_c t).
A band-pass filter becomes an equivalent low-pass filter acting on x̃(t).
Multiplication by a carrier becomes a simple frequency shift; downconversion and upconversion become multiplication by e^(∓j2πf_c t).
AWGN stays white and Gaussian in the low-pass model, so SNR results carry over directly.
Saves work: no carrier term in every equation, and simulation can run at baseband with a much smaller sampling rate.
State the narrowband condition B ≪ f_c.

bank.q: Derive the canonical representation of a real band-pass signal in terms of its in-phase and quadrature components, and state the properties of their spectra.
outline: Write the band-pass signal as x_c(t)cos(2πf_c t) − x_s(t)sin(2πf_c t) and recover x_c, x_s by low-pass filtering after multiplying by 2cos and 2sin.
Show x_c = x_I and x_s = x_Q, with the minus sign coming from the Hilbert pair.
Spectra of x_c and x_s are low-pass, of width B, and are related through the Hilbert transform.
Real x(t) gives a spectrum with conjugate symmetry about 0 Hz.
Applications: I-Q modulators, SDR front ends, image rejection.

bank.q: Distinguish between uncorrelated and statistically independent random variables, and justify the Gaussian model for receiver noise using the central limit theorem.
outline: Uncorrelated: E[XY] = E[X]E[Y], which for Gaussian variables also implies independence.
Independence is the stronger condition on the joint CDF.
Thermal noise comes from the summed motion of very many electrons, so the sum tends to a Gaussian amplitude by the central limit theorem.
The Gaussian PDF is fixed by only its mean and variance, which makes the analysis tractable; it is preserved by linear filtering.
Limits of the model: impulse and burst noise, interference, and non-Gaussian sources need other descriptions.

bank.q: Describe the main sources of noise in a communication receiver and distinguish between noise generated inside the device and interference picked up from outside.
outline: Thermal noise from random electron motion in a resistor, PSD = kT, rises with temperature.
Shot noise from the discrete arrival of charge carriers across a junction, proportional to direct current.
Flicker (1/f) noise at low frequencies, from traps and imperfections; dominant below a corner frequency.
Burst noise, random step-like jumps caused by defects.
External interference: other transmitters, mains hum, ignition noise, crosstalk.
Consequence for the designer: filter the band, lower the temperature or use a low-noise front-end, and keep the first-stage gain high.

glossary.def: The process of varying a parameter of a high-frequency carrier in proportion to a message signal.
A signal whose spectrum begins near 0 Hz and ends at some finite upper frequency W.
A signal whose spectrum is concentrated around a carrier frequency f_c far above 0 Hz.
The width in hertz of the frequency range that a signal or channel actually occupies or passes.
A device that converts one form of energy to another, such as a microphone turning sound into voltage.
The reduction in signal power as it travels through a channel, usually expressed in decibels.
Another name for the analytic signal x(t) + jx̂(t), which contains only positive frequencies.
The part of a band-pass signal that multiplies cos(2πf_c t), written x_I(t).
The part of a band-pass signal that multiplies sin(2πf_c t), written x_Q(t), shifted by 90 degrees from the in-phase part.
The probability-weighted average of a random variable, E[X] = ∫x f_X(x)dx.
The average squared deviation from the mean, σ² = E[X²] − (E[X])²; its square root is the standard deviation.
A variable whose PDF is (1/(σ√(2π)))·e^(−(x−m)²/(2σ²)), fully described by its mean m and variance σ².
A stationary process in which the time average of one long sample equals the ensemble average.
Noise produced by the random motion of electrons in a conductor, with two-sided PSD about kT/2 watts per hertz.
Noise caused by the discrete arrival of charge carriers, with mean square current 2eI·B.
Noise whose PSD falls roughly as 1/f, important in semiconductor devices at low frequencies.
Step-like noise jumps caused by impurities or defects, also called popcorn noise.
The width of an ideal rectangular filter that would pass the same total white-noise power as the real filter.
The ratio of signal power to noise power at a stated point, in watts per watt or in decibels.
The cascade relation F = F₁ + (F₂ − 1)/G₁ + (F₃ − 1)/(G₁G₂) + … for the total noise figure of stages in series.
The standard temperature T₀ = 290 K used to convert between noise figure and noise temperature.
The amplitude level at which a receiver decides which symbol was sent, fixed by the noise statistics.
The statement that the energy of a signal equals the integral of its spectral energy density over frequency.
Moving a signal's spectrum from one band to another, done by multiplying with a carrier or a local oscillator.
